title: Teresa's day (15 October)
hookLine: her bookmark: let nothing disturb you, God alone suffices

lines: A SLIP OF PAPER IN A PRAYER BOOK.
cards: A slip of paper, small enough to mark a page, with a few lines on it in Spanish. Tradition says it was found tucked in the prayer book of a nun from Ávila after she died, and that she had kept it there to read.
The lines say: don't be disturbed, don't be afraid, everything passes. And at the bottom, three words that people still copy onto cards and walls.
The nun was Teresa of Ávila, and the Catholic Church keeps her feast in October. Today, Teresa's day, and the words on her bookmark.

teach.b: Here are the lines, in a plain paraphrase. Let nothing disturb you. Let nothing frighten you.
All things are passing. God does not change. Patience gains everything.
Whoever has God lacks nothing. God alone is enough.

teach.h: SOLO DIOS BASTA: GOD ALONE IS ENOUGH.
teach.b: In Spanish, that last line is three words: solo Dios basta. Basta is the word you'd shout to stop an argument: enough! Teresa turns it around.
Not enough of this. Enough, because of God. Notice what the bookmark doesn't say.
Not that nothing bad will happen, but that things will pass. Not don't feel, but don't let it take you over.

Tradition remembers her life as busy and bumpy, with hard travel, illness and opposition, and the bookmark reads like something kept close because it was needed. The Bible has the same note in more than one place.
A psalm: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." I won't lack anything.

teach.h: MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.
teach.b: And Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, says that when he begged to be rid of some weakness, the answer came: "My grace is sufficient for thee." Sufficient. Enough.
Catholics honor Teresa as a saint and a teacher of prayer, and some Anglicans and Lutherans remember her too.
But the bookmark is for anyone who has stood in a kitchen at two in the morning, heart racing over a bill or a test result. It doesn't argue. In Teresa's voice, it just says: this will pass.

how: Catholics keep Teresa of Ávila's feast in October with readings from her writings, and some Anglicans and Lutherans remember her too; her bookmark lines are often printed on cards and prayed or sung, as in a Taizé chant.

it says all things are passing, and God does not change.
the last line, in Spanish, is three words
solo Dios basta: God alone is enough.

the answer came: my grace is sufficient for thee.

games.q: it's two in the morning and you can't stop worrying. you have Teresa's bookmark. which line does it end on?
games.why: it ends: God alone suffices. solo Dios basta. not a promise that things will be fine, but that God is enough.

practice: On a scrap of paper, a receipt or a sticky note, write the line from Teresa's bookmark you need today: let nothing disturb you, all things are passing, or God alone suffices; if you don't share her faith, all things are passing is a good one.
Read it slowly three or four times, then tuck it in a book you're reading. If you pray, hold your worries up against it one at a time; if you don't, let the line sit beside them.
